items.title: Building a Cross-Platform Qibla Experience with GeoQibla
items.author: Shahid Iqbal
items.description:
How a small Kotlin Multiplatform library turns sensor logic, permissions, alignment, and UI into a reusable Compose experience for Android and iOS

Most Qibla features look deceptively simple from the outside. Open the screen, point the device, and guide the user toward the right direction. But a production-grade implementation is never just a compass. It has to handle location permission, disabled location services, missing location fixes, unreliable heading data, calibration prompts, device tilt, recovery actions, localization, and the subtle difference between being near the Qibla and being precisely aligned with it. GeoQibla approaches that full problem as a reusable product surface, not a one-off widget. (GeoQibla)

GeoQibla is documented as a Kotlin Multiplatform Compose library for Qibla direction UI on Android and iOS, and the current docs present it as version 0.0.4, published under the dependency io.github.shahidzbi4213:geoqibla:0.0.4. The library is designed for shared Compose UI in commonMain, with Android support starting at API 26 and iOS relying on Core Location plus when-in-use location permission. (GeoQibla)

What makes GeoQibla interesting is its integration model. You can adopt it at two very different levels. At the high level, there is GeoQiblaScreen, a ready-made screen that renders a full compass flow. At the lower level, there is QiblaController, whose state is exposed as StateFlow<QiblaState> for teams that want to build a fully custom interface. That split matters. It means the same library can serve both fast-moving product teams that want a drop-in solution and engineering teams that need complete UI ownership. (Shahid Zbi)

In practice, the quickest path is very small:

implementation("io.github.shahidzbi4213:geoqibla:0.0.4")
val controller = rememberQiblaController()
GeoQiblaScreen(controller = controller)

That is essentially the quick-start story described in the docs: create the controller inside Compose, render the screen, and let the default UI manage the lifecycle by starting the controller when the composable enters composition and stopping it when it leaves. For a feature that depends on live location and heading streams, that built-in lifecycle handling is more valuable than it first appears. (Installation)

Why this is more than a compass widget

The most revealing part of GeoQibla is its state model. QiblaState includes the top-level UI state, compass state, location state, sensor accuracy, orientation source, a started flag, and an optional error message. The documented QiblaUiState values cover the entire user journey: idle, requesting permission, permission required, denied, permanently denied, location disabled, locating, sensor unavailable, calibration needed, tilted, ready, near Qibla, aligned, and error. That is not just presentation logic. It is a full runtime model for an interaction that spans sensors, permissions, and recovery flows. (States)

The architecture docs make that even clearer by describing a resolver priority for the UI. Errors outrank everything. Missing permission appears before location readiness. Missing location fix appears before heading readiness. Tilt and calibration warnings can interrupt an otherwise working compass. Stable alignment outranks “near Qibla,” and “near Qibla” outranks the general ready state. In other words, GeoQibla is explicitly designed to answer the real product question: what should the user see right now? (Architecture)

That detail shows up again in QiblaConfig. By default, the library treats the user as near the Qibla within 10 degrees, but it only declares full alignment when the heading remains within 3 degrees for 750 milliseconds. It also exposes smoothing for heading updates, a tilt limit of 55 degrees, magnetic field warning thresholds, optional haptics, and an onAligned callback. This is a strong design choice because it separates “roughly correct” from “stably correct,” which is much closer to how a user actually experiences directional guidance. (Configuration)

Under the hood, the library’s QiblaMath layer is documented as handling the bearing to the Kaaba, distance to the Kaaba, normalized compass degrees, shortest angular distance, magnetic-to-true azimuth conversion, and smoothed heading values. That means the value proposition is not limited to UI composition; GeoQibla also packages the numerical logic that usually gets scattered across platform-specific utility code. (Archtitecture)

A clean Kotlin Multiplatform architecture

From an engineering perspective, GeoQibla is a solid example of how a Kotlin Multiplatform library should be structured. The docs describe a common public API in shared code and platform-specific service implementations behind internal abstractions. The common layer contains the screen, controller, config, state models, styling models, slots, and reusable composables. The platform layer handles permission requests, location observation, orientation observation, settings recovery, and haptics. (Archtitecture)

On Android, GeoQibla uses LocationManager for last-known and live location updates, SensorManager with rotation vector when available, accelerometer plus magnetic field sensors as a fallback, and GeomagneticField to convert magnetic azimuth to true north when declination data is available. The default Android flow also uses Activity Result APIs for runtime permission and settings intents for recovery. On iOS, the library uses CLLocationManager, prefers trueHeading when available, falls back to magneticHeading, maps Core Location authorization into shared access states, and uses the app settings URL for recovery. One candid detail in the docs is that alignment haptics are implemented on Android, while performAlignmentHaptic() is currently a no-op on iOS. (Platform-Behaviour)

That architecture gives the project a useful balance: a single shared API for product code, with honest platform-specific handling where sensors and permissions differ. It is the kind of design that makes KMP feel practical rather than ideological. The shared code owns the contract and the state machine; the platform code owns the messy parts of the operating system. (Archtitecture)

The default screen is opinionated in the right places

The default screen looks designed for immediate shipping. According to the docs, it adapts between compact and wide layouts based on available width, uses safe content padding to avoid system bars, and composes the experience from a top bar, compass, state message, action area, and status rows. Its message panel maps QiblaUiState into localized copy, while its action buttons are already wired to controller methods such as start(), requestPermission(), retryLocation(), openLocationSettings(), openAppSettings(), and dismissCalibration(). (Defaults)

That matters because good recovery UX is usually the first thing missing from sensor-driven features. A user denies permission once, or has location services disabled, or the heading becomes unreliable, and a beautiful compass becomes a dead screen. GeoQibla’s default UI is built around recovery as a first-class concern. It does not merely detect failure states; it gives the user a path back from them. (Defaults)

Customization without starting over

Where GeoQibla becomes especially useful for real products is its customization model. The screen accepts QiblaStyle, QiblaStrings, and QiblaSlots directly. QiblaStyle groups colors, dimensions, typography, shapes, and animation timings. QiblaStrings provides English and Arabic variants, and the Arabic strings switch the layout direction to RTL for the entire screen. The docs also note that every visible label and action in the default UI comes from QiblaStrings, which is exactly what you want in a library that may land in multilingual apps. (Styling)

QiblaSlots adds a second layer of flexibility. Instead of forcing teams to rewrite the whole screen, it lets them surgically replace regions such as the top bar, compass dial, target badge, status rows, state message, calibration sheet, or action buttons. That is a smart middle ground between “take it exactly as-is” and “rebuild everything yourself.” Many product teams do not need a brand-new compass engine; they only need the screen to fit their own design system and user journey. (Components)

And when the default screen is too opinionated, the headless path is already there. The custom UI guide shows the intended pattern clearly: collect controller.state, start and stop the controller with Compose lifecycle, and render based on state.uiState, state.compass, and state.location. GeoQibla also exposes reusable building blocks like QiblaCompassDial, QiblaStateMessage, and QiblaStatusPanel, so even a custom screen can reuse the library’s tested primitives instead of discarding them. (Customization)

Developer experience is small, but pragmatic

The installation flow is intentionally lean: add the dependency to commonMain, sync Gradle, build the shared module, and validate on a device. The docs are also appropriately explicit about testing: simulators and emulators are useful for layout and permission-state validation, but final compass behavior should be checked on physical hardware. The Android example says the same for sensor and magnetic-field behavior, and the iOS example says the same for heading validation on a real iPhone. That is the kind of guidance that prevents false confidence during development.

On the platform setup side, Android expects coarse and fine location permissions in the merged manifest, while iOS requires NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription in Info.plist. None of that is unusual, but the fact that the docs keep it close to the quick-start flow reduces friction for the first integration. (Shahid Zbi)

Why GeoQibla is a good KMP case study

Even beyond the specific Qibla use case, GeoQibla is a useful example of a mature small library. The architecture docs call out shared tests for Qibla math, config validation, UI state resolution, and alignment tracking. The contribution guide lists local checks for shared tests, Android assembly, and strict docs builds. And the project is published under Apache License 2.0, which lowers friction for teams evaluating whether they can adopt it commercially.

That combination — shared API, platform-specific sensor integrations, explicit state modeling, careful customization points, and documented test coverage — is what gives a library like this credibility. Many cross-platform libraries stop at the demo stage. GeoQibla reads more like a deliberately packaged runtime surface: something meant to be embedded, branded, localized, and maintained inside real applications.

Closing thoughts

GeoQibla is best understood not as a compass component, but as a complete Qibla interaction layer for Kotlin Multiplatform apps. It offers a default screen for immediate integration, a controller-driven state flow for custom UI, configurable alignment behavior, platform-aware permission and sensor handling, reusable composables, localization support including Arabic RTL, and slot-based customization for product-specific layouts. For teams building prayer, travel, Islamic lifestyle, or utility apps, that is a meaningful reduction in engineering surface area.

In a broader sense, the project also illustrates where Kotlin Multiplatform is strongest: not merely sharing business logic, but sharing user-facing interaction systems that depend on real platform services while still respecting platform differences. GeoQibla packages that idea into a focused, practical library — and that is what makes it worth paying attention to.

items.title: What is Suspended function in kotlin?
items.author: Shahid Iqbal
items.description:
In Kotlin, a suspend function is a special type of function that can be paused and resumed later, allowing for asynchronous and non-blocking execution. Suspend functions are used in coroutines to manage concurrency and avoid blocking the main thread, which is important in Android for ensuring smooth and responsive user experiences.

A suspend function is defined using the suspend keyword and can only be called from within another suspend function or from a coroutine. When a suspend function is called, it can pause its execution and return control to the caller, while preserving its state. The function can later be resumed and continue its execution from where it left off.

suspend fun delaying() {
        //Code
}

Here’s an example of how a suspend function can be used in Android to fetch data from a network:

suspend fun fetchData(): List<Data> {
    // Code to fetch data from network
    // ...
    return dataList
}

In this example, the fetchData function is defined as a suspend function and can be used to fetch data from a network. The function can be called from a coroutine, which allows it to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the main thread. The data can then be used to update the UI or perform other actions as needed.

Note that the suspend function must be called from a coroutine or another suspend function. In Android, this can be achieved by using the launch or async functions, for example:

GlobalScope().launch {
    val data = fetchData()
    // Use data to update UI, etc.
    withContext(Dispatchers.Main) {
        // Update UI here
    }
}

Well That’s All For Now Bye Bye!!
